processing: Little is recorded about this tea's method in detail. As with other Zhejiang greens, expect fresh leaf fixed with heat to stop oxidation, then shaped and dried; the name points to a curled, downy leaf.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Zhejiang greens, with the earliest pickings normally prized.
appearance_dry: The name, 'curled down', suggests curled leaf with visible hairs; exact grade standards are not well recorded.
appearance_liquor: As is typical of Zhejiang spring greens, a pale, clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: As with other bud-rich spring greens, expect soft, tender green leaf.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting record is available for this tea. Zhejiang spring greens of this kind are usually fresh and lightly vegetal with a gentle sweetness.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for a tender Chinese green: cooler water and a glass or an open gaiwan, so the leaf does not stew.

vintage_note: Like other Chinese greens, it is normally bought as the current year's spring harvest and drunk within about a year. Earlier spring pickings usually cost more. No year-by-year market for this tea is recorded.
description:
Fenghua Quhao is a green tea from Fenghua in Ningbo, on the eastern side of Zhejiang. It is listed among Fenghua's Chinese geographical indication products, and that local standing is the clearest thing known about it.

The name reads simply: qu for curled, hao for fine down. Details of how it is made are scarce, so treat it as you would other Zhejiang spring greens, where the heat of fixing and the shaping decide most of what ends up in the cup.

Exact tasting notes for this tea are hard to pin down. A sensible expectation from its class is a light, fresh and gently sweet cup, best with cooler water and short attention.

When buying, ask for the harvest date and for Fenghua as the place of origin, since the name carries the local claim. It also appears on Zhejiang's promoted tea-tourism routes in the eastern part of the province, alongside Pubu Xianming and Wanghai tea, which are worth trying next to it.
history: Little is documented about the origin of Fenghua Quhao. What can be said is that it holds Chinese geographical indication status as a Fenghua product and is named in Zhejiang tea-tourism promotion. No reliable date or founder for the tea has been established.
